readerTitle: Dollar Shave Club's $4,500 video: a great launch, but not a growth plan
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Dollar Shave Club, Unilever) + 가상 적용 (대기업 마케팅팀, 동네 배관 업체)
insight: 바이럴 히트는 고객을 싸게 얻는 일회성 급등이다. 성장 계획은 다음 달에도 비슷한 비용으로 다시 살 수 있는 채널 위에 세운다.
misconception: 한 번 터진 영상의 고객당 비용이 우리 회사의 실제 고객 획득 비용이다. 바이럴 하나면 광고비 없이 계속 클 수 있다.

sources.text: DollarShaveClub.com launch video, "Our Blades Are F***ing Great", YouTube (March 2012)
Michael Dubin interviews in business press (e.g. Inc., Forbes) on the video's roughly $4,500 cost and about 12,000 orders in the first 48 hours
Unilever press release on acquiring Dollar Shave Club (July 2016); deal value widely reported as about $1 billion
Unilever announcement on selling a majority stake in Dollar Shave Club to Nexus Capital Management (2023)

factChecks.note: 영상 제작비 약 $4,500, 48시간 내 약 12,000건 주문은 창업자 인터뷰를 통해 널리 보도된 수치입니다. '주문'인지 '가입자'인지 매체마다 표현이 다릅니다. 카드에는 "reportedly"와 "orders"로 적었으니 게시 전 1차 인터뷰로 확인하세요.
계산: $4,500 ÷ 12,000 = $0.375. 카드에는 약 $0.38, "under 40 cents"로 표기했습니다. 영상 제작비만 포함한 수치이며 인건비, 배송, 제품 원가는 빠져 있습니다.
출시 이후 투자 유치와 TV 등 유료 광고에 큰 비용을 썼다는 내용은 널리 보도되었습니다. 구체적 금액은 출처마다 달라 카드에는 넣지 않았습니다.
Unilever 인수(2016년, 약 10억 달러로 보도)와 2023년 Nexus Capital Management에 과반 지분을 매각한 사실은 게시 직전 보도자료로 다시 확인하세요.
조회수는 "millions of views"로만 적었습니다. 정확한 수치와 시점은 자료마다 다릅니다.

cards.title: A $4,500 video and 12,000 orders in two days
body: In March 2012, an unknown razor startup posted a short video. Its founder, Michael Dubin, walks through a warehouse, deadpan, joking about overpriced razors.

The video reportedly cost about $4,500. Within 48 hours, reportedly about 12,000 orders came in, and the website struggled to keep up. It was one of the most famous launches of its decade. It was also not the way the company kept growing.

image.label: A founder joking in a warehouse while orders pile up
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 창고 안 선반 사이에서 정장 입은 남자가 카메라를 보며 무표정하게 말하고, 옆에 주문 상자가 폭포처럼 쏟아짐. 화면 구석에 서버 과열을 뜻하는 연기 나는 노트북. 실제 브랜드 로고, 제품 상표 사용 금지.

cards.title: The video is a hit. Now plan next year.
body: It's 2012. Your funny launch video has millions of views and brought thousands of orders in two days. Investors are calling.
How do you plan the next year of growth?

options.text: Make a new video every month. If one hit, more will
options.feedback: Videos are cheap to make, but hits can't be scheduled. You'd build a growth plan on a number you may never see again.

options.text: Treat the video as a head start, and build channels you can pay for again and measure
options.feedback: You keep the buzz as a bonus and plan on costs you can predict. You give up the dream of free growth, but you get a plan that still works when the buzz fades.

options.text: Spend nothing more. A brand people love this much will spread by word of mouth
options.feedback: Word of mouth is cheap and real, so it helps. But buzz fades in weeks, and without other channels growth slows with it.

cards.title: The video opened the door. Paid ads kept it open.
body: Dollar Shave Club kept its funny voice and made more videos. None became the growth engine on its own.
Instead, the company raised money and spent heavily on paid advertising, including TV. It grew into a large subscription business. In 2016, Unilever bought it for a reported **$1 billion**.
The famous video got the company noticed. Buying customers, month after month, is what built it.

cards.title: The launch math looks unbeatable.
cards.callout: Under 40 cents per order is a cost almost no ad channel offers. The catch: you get that number once, and you can't order a second one.

cards.title: A spike is not a channel.
body: A **repeatable channel** is a way of winning customers you can use again next month, at a cost you can roughly predict. Search ads, referrals and a sales team are examples.
A viral hit is a *spike*: very cheap, but you can't buy it again. If you mix spike customers into your average, your cost per customer looks far lower than what the next customer will cost.
So plan growth on repeatable channels. Count hits as a bonus, not a budget line.

image.label: A tall spike of orders fading, next to a steady line
image.brief: 선 그래프 인포그래픽. 주황색 선은 첫날 높이 치솟았다가 몇 주 만에 바닥으로 떨어짐("Viral spike"). 파란색 선은 낮지만 꾸준히 올라감("Paid channels you can repeat"). 로고 없음.

cards.title: "Make us a video like that."
body: The marketing team at a large insurer gets a request from leadership: make a viral video like Dollar Shave Club's, and cut the ad budget to pay for it.

A better brief keeps the paid channels running and gives the video a small, fixed budget. The team judges the year by cost per customer from channels it can repeat. If the video hits, that's a gift. If it doesn't, nobody's targets collapse.
cards.softwareNote: Apps see this after a launch-day spike from a product directory or a viral post. Those sign-ups flatter early cost per user. Judge the plan on cost per user from channels you can buy again, and on whether spike users stay.

cards.title: The hit still mattered, and it wasn't only luck.
body: The video worked because the offer was simple, cheap and a subscription. Customers kept paying each month, so each one was worth far more than one order. A funny video for a weak offer gets laughs, not sales.
A hit can also leave a lasting asset: a known name can make later ads work better. But fame guarantees nothing. In 2023, Unilever sold a majority stake in the business to an investment firm.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing business.
body: Your family plumbing company posts a funny clip of a DIY repair gone wrong. It gets hundreds of thousands of views. Calls double for two weeks, then start to fade.

options.text: Hire two more plumbers now to keep up with the new demand
options.feedback: You'd handle the rush, but you'd be adding fixed salaries based on a spike that's already fading.

options.text: Keep posting for fun, but set budgets by what local ads and referrals cost per booked job
options.feedback: You keep the upside of more clips while planning on costs you know. You may grow slower on paper, but the plan survives a quiet month.

options.text: Move half your local ad budget into making more videos
options.feedback: Videos may build a local name over time. But you'd trade a known cost per booked job for the hope of another hit.

cards.title: Bank the hit. Plan on what you can repeat.
body: A viral moment gives you cheap customers once. Your real cost per customer is what the next one costs through a channel you can use again.
**Try it today:** list where your last 20 customers came from. Mark each source you could buy again next month, and roughly what it would cost.
